title: Life under the Nazis, 1933–1939
description: Economic control, women, education, the Hitler Youth and the treatment of the Jews to 1939.
content_html:
The Nazi Economy, 1933–1939

One of the Nazis' most important early successes was tackling unemployment. When Hitler came to power in January 1933, approximately six million Germans were out of work. By 1938 unemployment had fallen to under half a million. How was this achieved? Partly through public works programmes — building the autobahn motorway network — and rearmament, which pumped money into heavy industry. The government also removed women from statistics by encouraging them to leave the workforce, and conscription from 1935 reduced the number of men counted as unemployed.

Finance minister Hjalmar Schacht managed the economy between 1933 and 1937, using a 'New Plan' (1934) to manage imports and exports and 'mefo bills' — government IOUs — to fund rearmament secretly without appearing to breach the Treaty of Versailles. From 1936 Hermann Göring supervised the Four Year Plan, designed to make Germany self-sufficient (autarky) and war-ready within four years. By 1939 Germany had substantially rearmed but had not achieved autarky.

Key Fact

Unemployment fell from approximately 6 million in 1933 to under 500,000 by 1938. However, real wages for workers barely recovered to 1929 levels, and the regime's economic growth depended heavily on rearmament spending — not sustainable peacetime prosperity.

Control of Workers: the DAF

In May 1933 the Nazis banned all independent trade unions and replaced them with the German Labour Front (DAF). Workers could no longer strike or negotiate freely. The 'Strength through Joy' (KdF) programme offered workers subsidised leisure activities — concerts, theatre, sports facilities and holidays — as a means of building loyalty and managing morale without granting genuine economic power. The 'Beauty of Labour' programme improved some factory conditions. In practice, workers gained material benefits but surrendered all collective bargaining rights.

Women in Nazi Germany: The Three Ks

The Nazis had a clearly defined role for women: Kinder, Küche, Kirche — children, kitchen, church. Women were expected to leave paid employment, marry, and bear as many children as possible to grow the German 'racial community'. The regime offered financial incentives: a marriage loan of 1,000 Reichsmarks was offered when women left work, with a quarter written off for each child born. By 1939 the birth rate had risen modestly compared to the early 1930s, though it never reached Nazi targets.

Women were removed from professional positions — female doctors, lawyers and civil servants were pushed out during 1933–1935. However, the ideology was pragmatic: as rearmament created labour shortages, women were gradually drawn back into the workforce from the late 1930s, demonstrating the tension between Nazi ideology and economic reality.

Nazi ideology reshaped the school curriculum. History was rewritten to glorify Germany's past and Hitler's role. Biology taught racial theory — the supposed superiority of the 'Aryan' race and the danger of 'inferior' groups. Physical education expanded, reflecting the Nazi emphasis on military fitness. Jewish teachers were dismissed. Textbooks were replaced with Nazi-approved versions. Teachers were required to join the National Socialist Teachers' League and teach approved content. By 1936 around 97% of teachers had joined the organisation.

The Hitler Youth

Outside school, the Hitler Youth organised boys from 14 to 18, with the Jungvolk for younger boys. Girls aged 14–18 joined the League of German Girls (BDM), focused on fitness and preparation for motherhood. Membership was made compulsory in 1936. Activities included camping, sports, marching and patriotic songs, all designed to build physical fitness and loyalty to Hitler. Many young Germans embraced the movement enthusiastically; others found the discipline oppressive. By 1939 the Hitler Youth had approximately eight million members.

Key Fact

Hitler Youth membership was made compulsory in 1936. By 1939 it had around eight million members. However, some young Germans resisted — the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth groups rejected Nazi conformity, listening to American music and challenging Hitler Youth authority.

The Treatment of Jews, 1933–1939

Antisemitism was central to Nazi ideology. From 1933 onwards the regime introduced a series of increasingly severe measures targeting Germany's Jewish population, which numbered approximately 500,000 — less than 1% of the German population. Jews were dismissed from civil service jobs under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933). Jewish-owned businesses were boycotted. Jews were excluded from cultural, legal and academic life.

In September 1935, the Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage and sexual relationships between Jews and non-Jews ('racial pollution'). Jews were defined by ancestry — anyone with three or four Jewish grandparents was classified as Jewish. By 1938, approximately 150,000 Jews had emigrated, but many lacked the money or the receiving country's willingness to take them.

On the night of 9–10 November 1938, a wave of violence swept across Germany and Austria. Approximately 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were destroyed, around 1,400 synagogues were burned, at least 91 Jews were killed, and approximately 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The event became known as Kristallnacht — the 'Night of Broken Glass'. Although presented as a spontaneous public reaction to the assassination of a German diplomat, Kristallnacht was organised with Nazi Party involvement. It marked a sharp escalation in the persecution of Jews, foreshadowing the more systematic violence to come.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark significance questions on the Nuremberg Laws or Kristallnacht, remember to address significance at the time (e.g. legal stripping of citizenship; immediate terror and property destruction) AND over time (part of a widening persecution that escalated to the Final Solution). For 16-mark essays on Nazi social policy, structure your response around distinct groups (workers, women, youth, Jews) and reach an overall judgement — for example on whether economic control or racial policy was more central to Nazi rule.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Nazis tackled unemployment through public works and rearmament, reducing it from ~6 million (1933) to under 500,000 (1938), but real wages barely recovered and growth was driven by unsustainable military spending.
  • Social policy enforced rigid gender roles (the Three Ks for women), reshaped education and made Hitler Youth compulsory from 1936, all aimed at creating a loyal, militaristic next generation.
  • Jews faced escalating persecution: dismissal from jobs (1933), the Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripping citizenship, and Kristallnacht (November 1938), marking a sharp intensification of state-organised violence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Nuremberg Laws (1935).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them stateless in their own country and denying them the rights of German citizens such as voting. [2 marks]
• The Nuremberg Laws banned marriage and sexual relationships between Jews and non-Jews, framed as preventing 'racial pollution', a concept central to Nazi racial ideology. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Nazi policy towards women in the years 1933–1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The 'Three Ks' (Kinder, Küche, Kirche) policy encouraged women to leave paid work and focus on bearing children; marriage loans of 1,000 Reichsmarks were offered as financial incentive. [2 marks]
• Women were removed from professional positions — female doctors, lawyers and civil servants were pushed out in 1933–1935. However, labour shortages from the late 1930s meant women were increasingly drawn back into the workforce. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the worsening treatment of Jews in Germany between 1933 and 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation of the cause.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and links cause to wider Nazi ideology or policy escalation.
Example: Nazi racial ideology, which defined Jews as an inferior racial threat to the German 'Volksgemeinschaft' (people's community), provided the ideological justification for escalating persecution. Each piece of legislation built on the last: dismissal from jobs (1933) was followed by legal exclusion (Nuremberg Laws, 1935) and then physical violence (Kristallnacht, 1938). The regime also responded to opportunities — the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris in November 1938 was used as a pretext for Kristallnacht.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Kristallnacht (November 1938) for Germany's Jewish community.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores long-term consequences and links to later persecution.
Example: Kristallnacht dramatically accelerated Jewish emigration. Approximately 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps after the pogrom, and property losses were severe. The regime also fined the Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks for the damage. In the months after November 1938, emigration rates increased sharply. However, many of those who wanted to leave faced difficulty finding countries willing to accept refugees, leaving them trapped in Germany.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hitler Youth for Nazi control of Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what the Hitler Youth did.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs the Hitler Youth against other means of control (SS, propaganda, economic policy) and assesses how far it achieved its aims.
At the time: Built loyalty among young Germans; trained boys for military service; inculcated Nazi ideology from an early age.
Over time: Created a generation of soldiers and party members committed to Hitler; however, resistance groups (Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth) show the limits of the indoctrination.

practice_questions.text:
'Nazi economic policy was more successful than Nazi social policy in winning German support between 1933 and 1939.' How far do you agree?
In your answer consider economic and social policy and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited evidence.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Nuanced analysis weighing the range and depth of support generated by different policies; distinguishes genuine enthusiasm from coerced compliance.

For economic: Unemployment nearly eliminated by 1938; 'Strength through Joy' leisure benefits; visible public works created sense of national purpose.
For social: Many women resented removal from careers; Jewish persecution alienated some Germans; youth indoctrination generated both loyalty and resistance.
Judgement might argue economic recovery generated broader and more genuine support, while social policies divided opinion — though fear of the police state made dissent dangerous to express.

glossary_terms.definition: The 1936 Nazi economic programme, supervised by Göring, aimed at making Germany self-sufficient (autarky) and ready for war within four years.
The Nazi replacement for independent trade unions, which controlled workers' pay and conditions and offered leisure benefits through 'Strength through Joy'.
September 1935 laws that stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews.
The 'Night of Broken Glass', 9–10 November 1938, a nationwide pogrom in Germany and Austria targeting Jewish businesses, homes and synagogues.
The Nazi youth movement for boys aged 14–18, compulsory from 1936, which combined physical training with ideological indoctrination.
Hjalmar Schacht, Germany's finance minister 1933–1937, who managed Nazi economic recovery using deficit spending and secret borrowing instruments.
Kinder, Küche, Kirche (children, kitchen, church) — the Nazi ideology defining the proper domestic role of German women.
